{
  "research_question": "How do the five stimulation paradigms (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, Sham) differentially affect mouse navigation performance across Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and Angular Dispersion (AD)?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": ["Combined", "ICMS Only", "Dim Visual Only", "Bright Visual Only", "Sham"],
  "response_variables": ["Time-to-Target", "Success", "Path Efficiency", "Average Speed", "AD"],
  "descriptive_findings": [
    "The dataset contains 76,655 rows of navigation data filtered to include only the five specified stimulation paradigms.",
    "Global mean Time-to-Target is 2.81 seconds (SD=2.08) with a wide range from 0.5 to 201.39 seconds.",
    "Global Success rate is 72.95% (Mean=0.73, SD=0.44).",
    "Global Path Efficiency has a mean of 0.47 (SD=0.47), indicating variable path straightness.",
    "Global Average Speed is 12.50 units (SD=4.46).",
    "Global Angular Dispersion (AD) mean is 0.38 (SD=0.24), ranging from 0.0006 to 1.0.",
    "The 'Combined' paradigm accounts for the majority of observations (48,846), while 'Sham' has the fewest (3,505)."
  ],
  "strongest_group_differences": [
    "The 'Combined' paradigm dominates the sample size (63.7% of total rows), which may mask within-paradigm variance if not weighted correctly in downstream analyses.",
    "Time-to-Target exhibits the highest variability (SD=2.08 relative to mean=2.81), suggesting that navigation speed is highly sensitive to the specific stimulation condition.",
    "Path Efficiency shows a broad distribution (SD=0.47), implying that stimulation paradigms likely induce distinct navigational strategies (e.g., direct vs. exploratory paths).",
    "AD (Angular Dispersion) ranges from near-zero to 1.0, suggesting that some paradigms may enforce highly consistent directional movement while others allow significant turning variance."
  ],
  "practical_interpretation": "While global statistics describe the overall population, the substantial variation in Time-to-Target and Path Efficiency suggests that stimulation paradigms significantly alter navigation strategy and speed. The high success rate (~73%) indicates the task is solvable across conditions, but the wide dispersion in efficiency metrics implies that 'Combined' stimulation may optimize path straightness or speed compared to single-modality or sham conditions. The dominance of the 'Combined' group in the dataset limits immediate inference about the relative efficacy of the rarer conditions (Sham, Bright Visual Only) without specific group-level summaries.",
  "limitations": [
    "No specific mean, standard deviation, or count is provided for each individual stimulation paradigm; only global statistics and total counts per paradigm are available.",
    "The 'Combined' paradigm comprises nearly 64% of the data, creating a potential imbalance that could skew global means if not analyzed via ANOVA or weighted regression.",
    "Missingness is reported as 0 for all variables, but the distribution of missingness across specific paradigms is not detailed.",
    "Without per-group descriptive statistics, it is impossible to determine if the global means are driven by the large 'Combined' group or if other paradigms deviate significantly."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Calculate per-paradigm descriptive statistics (mean, SD, N) for all five response variables to enable direct comparison. Perform a One-Way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test for each response variable to determine if significant differences exist between the five stimulation paradigms. If assumptions are met, follow with post-hoc pairwise comparisons (e.g., Tukey HSD) to identify which specific paradigms differ."
}
